proof:
**Actual simplex inequality and its tight rows.** For a simplex with the stated incidences, let $H$ be the sum of the positive vertex heights, $a_j$ the positive height at $P_j$ divided by $H$, and $b_{jl}$ the magnitude of the negative height of cap $j$ at $P_l$ divided by $H$. Then $\sum_j a_j=1$ and $\sum_{j\ne l}b_{jl}=a_l$ by balance. The cap fraction $q_j=Q_j/k$ is the product of its incident edge cut fractions $a_j/(a_j+b_{jl})$. The pyramid altitude gives $\sigma_j=dQ_j/(Ha_j)$, hence $M=H/d$ and $f_j=d\bigl(\prod_{l\ne j}(a_j+b_{jl})\bigr)^{1/d}$.

Fix row $i$ and simultaneously average row and column labels over permutations fixing $i$. Write $A=a_i$, $B=\sum_{l\ne i}b_{il}/d$, and $t=(1-A)/d$. The other diagonals average to $t$, entries from the other rows into column $i$ to $A/d$, and the other off-diagonal entries outside row $i$ to $(t-B)/(d-1)$. The averaged channels are therefore $A+B$ in the selected row, and $1/d$ toward $i$ and $(1-A-B)/(d-1)$ in the other slots of each other row. The geometric mean is concave because it is the infimum of the linear forms $\sum_l r_l x_l/d$ with $r_l>0$, $\prod_l r_l=1$, by AM–GM. Thus averaging increases $f_i$ and the sum of the other $f_j$. The averaged selected value is $\bar f_i=d(A+B)<d$, since $B<t$. The other averaged values are all $((d-\bar f_i)/(d-1))^{(d-1)/d}$. These give equality at the averaged data and prove the desired inequality at the original data.

Equality in the row inequality forces equality both in the selected geometric-mean average and in each other geometric-mean average, because the two components of $\Phi_i$ are strictly increasing in the selected value and other sum. In geometric-mean averaging, equality means the positive vectors being averaged are proportional, since the minimizing $r_l$ for their mean must also be minimizing at each vector, and equality in AM–GM specifies $r_lx_l$ constant in $l$. This forces $b_{il}=B$ for all $l\ne i$. In each other row $j$ the channels not pointing to $i$ have a common value $V_j$, by permuting those coordinates while holding that row fixed. The ratio of its channel toward $i$ to $V_j$ is common to all $j\ne i$ by the same proportionality. The column sum at $j\ne i$ now reads $a_j=B+\sum_{l\ne i,j}(V_l-a_l)$, hence $V_j=B+\sum_{l\ne i}V_l-1+A$ for every $j\ne i$. Consequently these channels are equal across all other rows, and so are their channels toward $i$. In particular all other row values are equal. At a tight row write $f_i=x\in(0,d)$ and $f_j=z>0$ for all $j\ne i$, so $x+(d-1)z^p=d$.

**Loss derivatives.** Regard the row as a smooth function of positive raw data. The gradient in the $f$ variables has entries $1$ at $i$ and $z^{1/(d-1)}$ elsewhere at tight data. Its pairing with $f$ equals $C=x+dz^p=(d^2-x)/(d-1)$. Along a loss of $E$ from $k,Q_j$ only, $M'= -1/\sigma_j$ and
$$
\frac{f_l'}{f_l}=-\frac1{dk}+\frac1{\sigma_j M}
-\frac{d-1}{dQ_j}\mathbf 1_{l=j}.
$$
Since $f_j=U(Q_j/k)^{(d-1)/d}$ for $U=dk/(\sigma_jM)>0$, this gives
$$
dk\,\alpha_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
C(1-U)+(d-1)x^{-1/(d-1)}U^p & j=i,\\
C(1-U)+(d-1)U^p & j\ne i .
\end{cases}
$$
For $U>0$ the minima of the two expressions are $C-x(C/d)^d$ and $C-(C/d)^d$, at $U=x(C/d)^{d-1}$ and $U=(C/d)^{d-1}$, respectively. The first minimum is positive because $x C^{d-1}$ increases strictly on $(0,d)$ to $d^d$, with logarithmic derivative $1/x-1/C>0$. The second is positive because $C<d^2/(d-1)$ and $(d/(d-1))^{d-1}\le d$ by the binomial expansion, each of its $d$ terms being at most one. This proves positivity for every vertex. In dimension two the stated planar formula follows by using the gradient pairing with $f$ at arbitrary positive data in this same logarithmic differentiation.

**Simultaneous losses.** If $E_j$ is the volume lost from the unique region of cap $j$, the exact data satisfy $k(K)=k(T')-\sum E_j$, $Q_j(K)=Q_j(T')-E_j$ and $\sigma_j(K)=\sigma_j(T')$. Source hyperplanes have zero volume. For fixed $i$, continuity of the partial derivatives yields a ball around the data of $T$ within the positive domain where all negative partial derivatives are at least $a_{T,i}/2$. Strict incidence and source interior are open, and the cap products and section formula above give continuity of simplex data. Restrict $T'$ to a smaller data ball and then take $E$ so small that the entire straight loss segment remains in the larger ball, using the bound $\sqrt2 E$ on its displacement. Integrating the partial derivatives along this segment gives the displayed margin. The segment need only lie in the positive data domain. For the finitely many initially tight rows take the intersection of the permitted neighborhoods and loss ranges. Initially strict rows remain so by continuity. Every proper convex inner body loses positive volume, by strict separation of any omitted point and positivity of the resulting cap.

**Planar geometry.** On the edge joining $P_j,P_l$ the third cap margin is strictly negative. Balance therefore makes the two incident cap margins overlap on an interval of positive length between their distinct cut endpoints. The six endpoints occur in consecutive pairs on the three edges, and their hull contains those edge intervals and the source, since it contains all full cutting chords. Its complement in $T'$ consists, up to boundaries, of three corner triangles in unique-cap regions. Indeed the two margins other than the corner's own are nonpositive at all three vertices of that corner triangle, and strictly negative at the original vertex. Conversely equality of the full chords forces their six endpoints, hence their hull, into $K$. Containment of the hull forces equality of each chord because $K\subseteq T'$.

statement:
Let $d\ge2$, fix an interior mark $y$ and $d+1$ nonzero spanning normals $v_i$ with $\sum_i v_i=0$. For a convex body $K$ with $y$ interior, let $k$ be its volume, $Q_j$ its cap volumes in $v_j\cdot(x-y)\ge0$ and $\sigma_j$ the corresponding $(d-1)$-dimensional section measure divided by $\lVert v_j\rVert$. With $M=\sum_jQ_j/\sigma_j$ and $p=d/(d-1)$, put
$$
f_j=\frac{d k^{1/d}Q_j^{(d-1)/d}}{\sigma_j M},\qquad
\Phi_i=f_i+(d-1)\left(\frac{\sum_{j\ne i}f_j}{d}\right)^p .
$$
A simplex has strict distinct-vertex incidence if the open positive halfplane of each cap contains one vertex and its open negative halfplane contains every other vertex, with a different positive vertex for each cap.

Fix a strict distinct-vertex simplex $T$ with at least one tight row $\Phi_i(T)=d$. For every sufficiently nearby simplex $T'$ (in its ordered vertices) and convex body $K\subseteq T'$ with all actual section measures unchanged and with all lost volume confined, up to null sets, to the $d+1$ regions belonging to exactly one cap, put $E=|T'\setminus K|$. There is a fixed positive threshold for $E$ such that for every row tight at $T$,
$$
\Phi_i(K)\le\Phi_i(T')-\frac{a_{T,i}}2 E\le d-\frac{a_{T,i}}2 E,
\qquad a_{T,i}=\min_j \alpha_{ij}(T)>0 .
$$
Here $\alpha_{ij}(T)$ is the negative partial derivative at the data of $T$ obtained by subtracting the same loss from $k,Q_j$ with all sections fixed. The rows strict at $T$ remain strict, so all rows are strict when $E>0$.

In the plane the geometric premises on $K$ are guaranteed by $C_{T'}\subseteq K\subseteq T'$, where $C_{T'}$ is the convex hull of the six cutting-chord endpoints. Within the inner-body class, retaining the full cutting chords is equivalent to containing $C_{T'}$. For planar row $1$, writing $e_1=f_1$, $e_j=(f_2+f_3)f_j/2$ for $j\ne1$ and $C=\sum_j e_j$, one has $\alpha_{1j}=C/(2k)+e_j/(2Q_j)-C/(M\sigma_j)$ at $T$.
title: Uniform Lorentz row margins for fixed-section simplex corner losses
